headline: Scott asks Trump administration to let Vermont resettle more refugees
dek: The governor says Vermont can accommodate up to 300 fully vetted refugees in the new fiscal year, more than twice the roughly 125 arrivals the state is preparing for under current federal policy.
body: Vermont Gov. Phil Scott is asking the Trump administration to expand the number and range of refugees the state can receive in the federal fiscal year that began Oct. 1. Vermont is preparing for about 125 arrivals under its current allocation, but state officials say the resettlement system has capacity for as many as 300 fully vetted refugees.

The request comes as the federal government sets the rules that determine whether Vermont’s capacity can be used. In a [statement carried by Vermont Business Magazine](https://vermontbiz.com/news/2026/october/02/scott-requests-president-increase-and-broaden-fully-vetted-refugee-admissions), Scott’s office said the governor sent President Donald Trump a letter seeking broader admissions for people fleeing war and persecution. The governor framed the request around both humanitarian concerns and the contributions refugees make to Vermont communities and the workforce.

The timing is significant because the [Federal Register’s FY2027 presidential determination](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/10/02/2026-20318/presidential-determination-on-refugee-admissions-for-fiscal-year-2027) authorizes the admission of up to 17,500 refugees nationwide. The document says those admissions will be allocated primarily among Afrikaners from South Africa and remain subject to other federal restrictions and case-by-case requirements. That national ceiling is not a Vermont quota, but it establishes the narrow federal pool from which state resettlement partners must work.

Independent reporting shows the practical gap Vermont is trying to close. [WCAX reported](https://www.wcax.com/2026/10/02/scott-asks-trump-administration-raise-vermonts-refugee-cap/) that Scott’s letter seeks to roughly double Vermont’s intake from 125 to about 250, while the governor’s announcement says the state could welcome up to 300. The difference reflects a distinction between the state’s current planning figure and its broader capacity: neither number guarantees that many people will arrive, because admission decisions and federal allocations remain outside Vermont’s control.

Vermont’s [State Refugee Office](https://humanservices.vermont.gov/our-work/programs-services/state-refugee-office) coordinates with resettlement organizations that help newly arrived families find housing, enroll children in school, navigate health care and enter the workforce. The office describes its mission as helping refugees and immigrants participate in the state’s economic, social and civic life, working through providers including the U.S. Committee for Refugees and Immigrants and the Ethiopian Community Development Council. That infrastructure is why the governor’s letter emphasizes capacity rather than asking Vermont to accept arrivals without a plan.

The issue also carries a local workforce and demographic dimension. WCAX quoted state refugee director Tracy Dolan describing young people and families with children as quickly becoming part of local communities and the economy. [WPTZ’s report](https://www.mynbc5.com/article/vermont-scott-trump-refugee-limits/73999506) likewise said Scott argued that refugees contribute to the state’s workforce and communities. Those are state-level claims, not a guarantee that every community or employer will experience the same effect, and the available reports do not provide a forecast of how many workers or students a larger intake would add.

The next decision belongs to federal officials. Vermont can prepare case managers, housing partners and schools for more arrivals, but it cannot set the national ceiling or determine which applicants receive refugee admission. Scott made a similar request in 2020, according to the governor’s office and WCAX. For this fiscal year, the unresolved question is whether the administration will approve a broader Vermont allocation consistent with the state’s stated capacity, and whether the federal admissions priorities will leave room for the mix of families Vermont is asking to welcome.
author: NorthEast News Desk
